questions.question: In round-robin load balancing, how are requests distributed across servers?
options: Each request goes to the server with the lowest current load
Requests are sent to servers in sequential, rotating order
Requests are randomly assigned to any available server
All requests go to the primary server until it's full
questions.explanation: Round-robin sends each new request to the next server in a fixed rotation: A, B, C, A, B, C, and so on. It doesn't consider current load or randomness.

questions.question: What is the key difference between Layer 4 and Layer 7 load balancing?
options: Layer 4 is faster; Layer 7 doesn't exist
Layer 4 operates on transport (TCP/UDP) data; Layer 7 operates on application (HTTP) data
Layer 4 works only with UDP; Layer 7 works only with TCP
Layer 7 is always slower and should be avoided
questions.explanation: Layer 4 load balancers route based on TCP/UDP information (IP, port), while Layer 7 load balancers can inspect HTTP headers, cookies, and URLs to make smarter routing decisions.

questions.question: In weighted round-robin, a server with weight 3 compared to servers with weight 1 will receive approximately:
options: The same amount of traffic as others
Three times as much traffic as a weight-1 server
One-third the traffic of a weight-1 server
Traffic only when other servers are busy
questions.explanation: Weighted round-robin assigns traffic proportional to each server's weight. A server with weight 3 receives three requests for every one request sent to a weight-1 server.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of health checks in load balancing?
options: To monitor how much CPU each server is using
To detect unresponsive servers and stop sending them traffic
To balance the load equally at all times
To encrypt traffic between the load balancer and servers
questions.explanation: Health checks periodically probe servers to verify they're responding. If a server fails a health check, the load balancer removes it from the active pool so no traffic is wasted on a dead server.

questions.question: Sticky sessions (session affinity) ensure that:
options: Sessions are evenly distributed across all servers at random
A user's requests always go to the same backend server
Sessions are stored in a shared database
The load balancer caches all session data locally
questions.explanation: Sticky sessions use cookies or IP hashing to route a user's subsequent requests to the same server, ensuring session state is preserved without shared storage.

questions.question: When a backend server fails, a properly configured load balancer will:
options: Crash and stop routing all traffic
Continue sending requests to the failed server hoping it recovers
Detect the failure via health checks and reroute traffic to healthy servers
Immediately restart the failed server
questions.explanation: A load balancer with health checks detects the failure, removes the dead server from the pool, and redistributes its traffic to the remaining healthy servers — often without users noticing.

questions.question: Least-connections load balancing sends new requests to the server that:
options: Has been running the longest
Was most recently added to the pool
Currently has the fewest active connections
Has the highest configured weight
questions.explanation: Least-connections tracks how many active connections each server has and routes new requests to the one with the fewest, preventing any single server from being overloaded.

questions.question: A single load balancer in front of your servers introduces:
options: No new risks at all
A single point of failure if the load balancer itself goes down
Guaranteed 100% uptime
The need to remove health checks
questions.explanation: A single load balancer is itself a single point of failure. Production systems typically use redundant (active-passive or active-active) load balancer pairs to mitigate this risk.

questions.question: Which load balancing algorithm is best suited when backend servers have significantly different hardware capabilities?
options: Round-robin
Random selection
Weighted round-robin or weighted least-connections
First-available
questions.explanation: Weighted algorithms let you assign higher weights to more powerful servers so they receive proportionally more traffic, making efficient use of heterogeneous hardware.

questions.question: An active health check differs from a passive health check in that:
options: Active checks are cheaper and never add network overhead
Active checks periodically send probe requests; passive checks monitor real traffic for errors
Passive checks are always more accurate than active checks
There is no difference; the terms are interchangeable
questions.explanation: Active health checks proactively send synthetic requests (like HTTP GETs to /health). Passive checks observe real user traffic and flag servers that return too many errors or timeouts.
